sph_ship_still.name: Floating Hull: Still Water
sph_ship_still.question: Are flotation and motion consistent with the body parameters?

layers.title: The question
layers.text: Are flotation and motion consistent with the body parameters?

layers.title: What the colours and motion show
layers.text: The rigid hull is placed on still water with the wavemaker stopped. It should settle to its equilibrium draught and its heave and roll should decay.

layers.title: One change to try
items: Change the ship size and compare the equilibrium draught.

layers.title: What to measure
layers.text: Heave settling to a constant and roll decaying to zero.
more: Then open the Floating Hull on Waves scene.

layers.title: Physical explanation
layers.text:
This exhibit runs six free-surface scenes from one solver — pick from the 'Scene' control: a dam break, a block dropped into a pool, a sloshing tank, pouring water into a glass, a wavemaker driving an ocean of waves, and a rigid ship floating on those waves. Each scene exposes its own controls (drop size and release height, slosh strength and period, spout width and pour speed, wavemaker stroke and period, ship size), so you can dial in the physics that matters for that scenario.

Take the dam break: hold back a column of water with a wall, remove the wall instantly, and gravity converts the column's potential energy into a fast horizontal surge. The front races along the floor, climbs the opposite wall, and overturns into a breaking jet. The free surface — the moving air–water boundary — folds over on itself, exactly the kind of large deformation and topology change that is painful for grid-based methods.

Smoothed-Particle Hydrodynamics takes a completely different, mesh-free view: the fluid is represented by a cloud of particles that carry mass and velocity and move with the flow (a Lagrangian description). Any continuous field — density, pressure, their gradients — is reconstructed at a particle by a smoothed, weighted sum over its neighbours within a smoothing length, using a bell-shaped kernel W. Because the particles simply follow the water, the free surface is wherever the particles happen to be — no interface tracking required.

Pressure is obtained from a stiff equation of state (weakly-compressible SPH): the fluid is treated as very slightly compressible so that small density changes produce the large pressures that resist compression. SPH is widely used for violent free-surface flows in coastal, marine and flood engineering.

layers.title: Equations, symbols and assumptions
layers.text:
• vi — velocity of particle i; Dvi/Dt is its acceleration following the flow
• mj — mass of neighbour particle j
• pi, pj — pressures (from the Tait equation of state); ρi, ρj — densities
• ∇Wij — gradient of the smoothing kernel between particles i and j; it carries the pressure force along the line joining them
• Πij — Monaghan artificial viscosity, added for stability at shocks/impacts
• g — gravity, the driving body force
• the walls are dynamic boundary particles: a fixed layer that feels the fluid pressure through the same equation of state and pushes back — a physical wall, not a penalty force, so the water near the walls behaves like the bulk

layers.title: Initial and boundary conditions (this preset)
layers.ic: Still water at 40 % fill with the rigid hull placed at the surface.
layers.bc: Fixed walls, the paddle held still (stroke 0); hull driven by contact forces from the water, gravity and damping, with motion limits.

layers.title: Numerical method, checks and limitations
layers.text: Weakly-compressible SPH: each particle carries mass and velocity; density and forces are smoothed sums over neighbours using a cubic-spline kernel. Pressure follows a stiff Tait equation of state (clamped ≥ 0 to avoid the free-surface tensile instability), with Monaghan artificial viscosity and a uniform background grid for fast neighbour search. The walls are dynamic boundary particles — fixed layers of particles that develop pressure through the same equation of state when the fluid presses on them, so the wall pushes back with real pressure (no penalty force on the fluid, no spurious near-wall motion); the wavemaker is simply a wall layer that moves. A δ-SPH density-diffusion term and XSPH velocity smoothing damp the acoustic noise and relax the initial lattice; the floating hull is a rigid body driven by contact forces from the fluid, gravity and damping, with limits on its motion.
layers.checks: Numerical check: free-decay behaviour; the hull is driven by contact forces from the water, gravity and damping, with limits on its motion — not by a pressure integration over the hull.

layers.title: References
items: Monaghan, J.J. (1994). Simulating free surface flows with SPH. J. Comput. Phys. 110, 399–406.

sph_ship.name: Floating Hull on Waves
sph_ship.question: How does the hull respond to the wave train?

layers.title: The question
layers.text: How does the hull respond to the wave train?

layers.title: What the colours and motion show
layers.text: The rigid hull rides the wavemaker's waves, heaving and rolling as the surface moves beneath it.

layers.title: One change to try
items: Change the wave period: the hull responds most near its own natural periods.

layers.title: What to measure
layers.text: Heave and roll records alongside the wave gauges.

scene.label: Scene
scene.help: Which free-surface scenario to run. Each scene exposes its own controls below. Still water is the hydrostatic baseline: nothing should move.

width.label: Dam width
width.help: Width of the held-back water column (tank 5 × 3.2 m).

height.label: Dam height
height.help: Height of the column — more head → a faster, taller surge.

dropsize.label: Blob diameter
dropsize.help: Diameter of the falling water blob (a parcel of water, not a capillary droplet — there is no surface tension in this model).

dropheight.label: Release height
dropheight.help: How high the blob starts, as a fraction of tank height (sets the impact speed √(2 g h)).

sloshA.label: Slosh strength
sloshA.help: Amplitude of the oscillating sideways gravity, as a multiple of g.

sloshT.label: Slosh period
sloshT.help: Period of the side-to-side forcing. Near the tank's natural period the wave resonates and breaks.

spout.label: Spout width
spout.help: Half-width of the pour stream as a fraction of the glass width. Values below 3 particle spacings are raised to that minimum (shown in derived quantities).

pourv.label: Pour speed
pourv.help: Speed the water leaves the spout. Faster → more splashing on impact.

waveA.label: Wavemaker stroke
waveA.help: Stroke of the wavemaker paddle (the wall's travel), which sets the wave amplitude indirectly — it is not the wave height itself. 0 = still paddle (free decay / equilibrium test for the ship).

waveT.label: Wave period
waveT.help: Period of the wavemaker — sets the wavelength of the train.

shipsz.label: Ship size
shipsz.help: Scale of the floating hull. Bigger ships sit deeper and roll slower.

particles.label: Particles (≈)
particles.help: Approximate number of SPH particles: sets the particle spacing dp (see derived quantities). More → finer splash, slower. The pour scene emits particles continuously and ignores this.

duration.label: Duration (×)
duration.help: Simulated interval as a multiple of the scene's reference interval (1.0 = default).
